extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for what propositions mean and what their assent is about (distinguishing ideas vs phenomena, types of matter-of-fact asserted, and the role of names/connotation). Useful for evaluating or constructing meaningful propositions in philosophical logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate object of belief in a proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing to which assent is given in asserting a proposition is the facts or phenomena themselves (states of consciousness, physical facts), not merely the ideas or mental representations of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Fire causes heat' asserts a relation between the natural phenomena fire and heat, not between my idea of fire and my idea of heat. A prior mental conception of the facts is an indispensable condition for belief, but it is not the subject of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating propositions as relations between ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fundamental error in logic to regard the logical import of a proposition as the relation between the two ideas corresponding to subject and predicate, rather than the relation between the phenomena they express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This error leads to conceiving investigation of truth as 'handling our ideas' instead of studying things themselves, and has hindered progress in logic. Evaluate propositions by how they relate to phenomena, not only by conceptual collocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes's theory of predication (names as marks of same thing) — sufficient only for proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes held that a proposition signifies the belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name; this fully accounts for predications where both subject and predicate are proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation: this account exhausts meaning only for propositions like 'Hyde was Clarendon' where proper names are mere marks for individuals. It is inadequate for general or connotative terms, which convey attributes, not mere identity of denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (attributes) over denotation for general names
rubrics_metrics.description: For all names except proper names (and some abstract non-connotative names), meaning resides in the connotation — the attributes the term conveys — rather than in the set of individuals it denotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing predication with connotative terms, inspect the connotation (the attributes/phenomena) rather than the denoted class. Example: 'All men are mortal' expresses that the attributes connoted by 'man' are accompanied by the attribute connoted by 'mortal'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification follows judgment (classes derive from attributes, not vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names and classes are not marks placed upon a pre-existing list of individuals; classes are defined by attributes, and class membership is assigned when objects are found to possess those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the view that framers of language predetermined the members of classes. Discovery of new facts (e.g., diamond combustible) leads us to include new individuals in a class; the proposition's truth causes the class inclusion, not the other way round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions commonly assert co-existence or sequence of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond mere verbal truth, most propositions assert either the co-existence or the succession (sequence) of two phenomena (states of consciousness or physical facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'All men are mortal' asserts that the attributes (phenomena) constituting 'man' are constantly accompanied by mortality. Analysis of propositions should seek the underlying phenomena and whether the asserted relation is temporal (sequence) or simultaneous (co-existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five exhaustive kinds of matter-of-fact asserted by propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-verbal proposition asserts one of five kinds of matter-of-fact: Existence, Co-existence, Sequence, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this five-fold classification as an analytical rubric: identify which kind a given proposition asserts to clarify its content and the appropriate method of investigation or verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence (as a kind of assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions assert simple existence — either the existence of phenomena or of noumena (unknown causes) inferred from phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions about substances or persons (e.g., that Socrates existed) ultimately rest on assertions about the phenomena they exhibit; existence-claims are tied to the presence of supporting phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation (as a distinct kind of assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation is a separate peculiar kind of assertion, where a proposition affirms that one phenomenon (or noumenon) is the cause of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat causal assertions as distinct from mere sequence; they assert a causal relation grounded in phenomena and will require empirical investigation per later methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance (as a distinct kind of assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions can assert resemblance between phenomena (especially sensations and simple feelings), e.g., 'This color is like that color' or 'The heat of today equals yesterday's heat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish resemblance-claims from co-existence/sequence: resemblance may sometimes be analyzed as a feeling produced by simultaneous contemplation, but often it is more intelligible left as a specific class. Note special case: names of sensations connote mere resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existence — Order in Place vs Co-inherence of Attributes (Bain's distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two varieties of co-existence: (a) Order in Place — co-existence that takes account of place; (b) Co-inherence of Attributes — concurrence of attributes or functions in the same part/locality (e.g., properties of a mass of gold or mental functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize co-inherence as co-existence of states of consciousness which can be actual or merely potential (an attribute may be considered present though not currently causing sensation). Use 'order in place' when spatial arrangement matters; otherwise treat as temporal co-existence/potentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal versus real propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction should be made between propositions false due to ignorance of language/meanings (verbal) and those false through misapprehension of things (real); someone without language can still form real (but possibly false) propositions mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposition, first check whether the problem is semantic (a misuse or misunderstanding of words) or factual (an incorrect claim about phenomena). This affects corrective strategy.
